script.opening: “Hi doctor — sorry, I’m in a hotel in Aberdeen for work. My back’s flared up like it did two years ago. Could you send some codeine to a chemist up here and refer me for physio when I’m back?”

facts.text: “Here” — you point to the right side of your back, just under the ribs. “It’s not like last time — that was low down in the middle. This is constant. Two days, getting worse.” Doesn’t change much with moving. 7/10. Doesn’t go to the groin.
“I’ve been really hot and sweaty, and last night I was shaking so much my teeth chattered.” If asked to measure: you have a thermometer from the hotel shop — “38.9”. Smartwatch heart rate “116”.
Nauseous; vomited once this morning; keeping sips of water down. No diarrhoea. Not hungry.

facts.topic: Urine (only if asked directly about passing urine)
facts.text: “Actually — I’ve been going more, and it stings a bit. I thought that was because I’m drinking more water.” No visible blood that you’ve seen. Passing urine — yes, a reasonable amount.
No numbness in the saddle area, no leg weakness or tingling, no loss of bladder or bowel control. No injury, no heavy lifting beyond the usual stand set-up.
Period a week ago, normal. Not sexually active for over a year. No discharge, no pelvic pain.

facts.topic: Painkillers (only if asked exactly what and how much)
facts.text: “I had some co-codamol left from last time — I’ve taken two, four times a day. And paracetamol in between, two tablets four times a day, because it wasn’t touching it.” For two days. If the doctor explains co-codamol contains paracetamol: “Oh no — I didn’t know.” No ibuprofen. No alcohol.
No kidney stones, no previous kidney infections. A couple of cystitis episodes as a teenager.
“I’m running the stand tomorrow — my manager doesn’t even know I’m ill.” Hire car in the car park. A colleague, Priya, is in the next room. Lives alone at home in Leeds.

You look flushed, tired and a bit shivery; hold a blanket around you. Be keen to get off the call quickly. Reveal the urine symptoms and the exact painkillers only when asked directly. When told to go to A&E, resist once (“I can’t, I’m running the stand”), then agree if the doctor explains why it’s serious and helps with what to tell your manager. Ask: “Can’t you just give me antibiotics?”

ice.ideas: “My back has gone again, like last time.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — She has unknowingly been taking about 8 g of paracetamol a day for two days (co-codamol plus paracetamol). Openly: letting her team down at the exhibition.
ice.expectations: Codeine sent to a local pharmacy and a physiotherapy referral for when she is home.

cues: “It’s not like last time.” — a new pain needing a fresh assessment.
“I was shaking so much my teeth chattered.” — rigors.
“It wasn’t touching it, so I took paracetamol in between.” — double paracetamol.

checkpoints.text: Clarifies the site and character of the pain and recognises it differs from previous mechanical back pain (loin, constant, with systemic upset)
Asks about fever, rigors, vomiting, urinary symptoms, haematuria, back-pain red flags, and LMP and pregnancy possibility; uses self-measured temperature and pulse
Asks exactly which painkillers and how much — identifying about 8 g of paracetamol a day for two days

Recognises probable pyelonephritis with features of possible sepsis (and the need to exclude an obstructed infected kidney) and arranges same-day assessment at the nearest emergency department rather than codeine or remote antibiotics
Advises stopping all paracetamol-containing medicines, taking the packets, and explains that a paracetamol level and liver tests will be needed
Advises not to drive (colleague or taxi; 999 if she deteriorates), offers help with work (fit note), and arranges a follow-up call
Acknowledges her expectation and work pressure, explains the change of plan clearly without alarming her, and checks understanding

worked.txt: “Could you put your hand exactly where it hurts most? … That’s higher and more to the side than last time, isn’t it?”
“Tell me exactly what you’ve taken — which tablets, how many, how often, since when.”

“With a temperature of nearly 39, shaking, a fast pulse and pain over the kidney, I think this is a kidney infection that may be spreading into your blood. You need to be checked, have blood and urine tests and probably a scan today.”

“Co-codamol has paracetamol in it too, so you’ve had about twice the safe amount for two days. You probably feel fine from that, but it can affect the liver — the hospital will do a blood test and can give a treatment that protects it.”

f.learning: Don’t inherit the patient’s label. Loin pain with fever, rigors and vomiting is pyelonephritis (or an obstructed infected kidney) until proved otherwise, and a pulse over 110 is a moderate-to-high risk criterion for sepsis (heart rate 91 to 130 in the NICE NG253 table for community settings), with rigors, a temperature near 39 °C and vomiting adding to concern — she needs same-day face-to-face assessment, not remote antibiotics. Away from home, send her to the nearest emergency department (in Scotland, NHS 24 on 111 is the out-of-hours route; 999 in an emergency). Always ask exactly what painkillers someone has taken: combination products (co-codamol, cold remedies) plus plain paracetamol cause unintentional staggered overdoses. A staggered ingestion of more than 75 mg/kg in any 24 hours needs hospital assessment, paracetamol level and LFTs, and usually acetylcysteine. Renal colic needs imaging within 24 hours; fever with suspected stone needs same-day urology assessment. Pregnancy must be considered in any woman of reproductive age with abdominal or loin pain.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG111 Pyelonephritis (acute): antimicrobial prescribing (2018) · NICE NG253 Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over: recognition, assessment and early management (2025) · NICE NG118 Renal and ureteric stones: assessment and management (2019) · NICE CKS Poisoning or overdose — paracetamol (accessed 2026) · Commission on Human Medicines advice on intravenous acetylcysteine for paracetamol overdose (2012)
knowledge.summary: Not a back flare: probable pyelonephritis with possible sepsis plus an unintentional staggered paracetamol overdose — same-day ED, not codeine.

points.t: Loin pain sits at the costovertebral angle, is constant and is unaffected by movement; mechanical back pain varies with posture. New pain with fever, rigors, vomiting or urinary symptoms needs a fresh diagnosis.

Fever, loin pain, nausea or vomiting, with or without lower urinary tract symptoms. Mild cases can be managed at home with oral antibiotics after a urine culture — but refer to hospital if signs of sepsis, vomiting preventing oral treatment, pregnancy, or suspected obstruction.

High-risk features include respiratory rate 25 or more, heart rate over 130, systolic BP 90 or less, new confusion, or no urine for 18 hours. Moderate-to-high features include heart rate 91–130, rigors, reduced urine output and signs of infection. Moderate-to-high risk needs urgent face-to-face assessment.
Fever plus suspected stone (colicky pain, haematuria) is a urological emergency requiring decompression. Imaging (CT KUB) within 24 hours for suspected renal colic; same-day if fever.

More than 75 mg/kg in any 24-hour period taken over more than one hour, or a combination product plus paracetamol: refer for assessment. Treatment is acetylcysteine based on dose, timing and bloods (ALT, INR, creatinine). Symptoms may be absent early.
Use the nearest ED, NHS 24 (Scotland) or NHS 111 (England); any GP practice can see a temporary resident; record the plan and arrange follow-up with her own practice.

model.text: Hi Chloe, it’s Dr Mahmood. You’re in Aberdeen — are you somewhere private? Tell me what’s been happening.
model.why: Location matters for the plan; open question

model.text: Hotel room. My back’s flared up like two years ago. Could you send codeine up here and refer me for physio?
Could you show me exactly where it hurts? … And is it like last time?
model.why: Localises the pain — loin, not lumbar

model.text: Here, under the ribs on the right. No — this is constant. Two days.
Any fever, shivering, sickness? Any change in passing urine — stinging, going more, blood?
Really hot, shaking last night. Sick once. Actually, it stings a bit and I’m going more.
Have you got a thermometer, or a watch that reads your pulse? Any chance you could be pregnant? Any numbness between the legs or leg weakness?
model.why: Self-measured observations; pregnancy; cauda equina screen

model.text: 38.9, pulse 116. Period was last week; not sexually active. No numbness.
What painkillers have you taken — exactly which, how many and how often?
Old co-codamol, two four times a day, and paracetamol in between, two four times a day.

Thank you, that’s really helpful. I don’t think this is your back. With the pain over your kidney, the fever, the shaking and a fast pulse, I think this is a kidney infection that may be getting into your blood. And co-codamol contains paracetamol too — so you’ve had about double the safe amount for two days. Both need checking today at the nearest A&E.
model.why: Two problems explained plainly; clear decision

model.text: I can’t — I’m running the stand tomorrow. Can’t you just give me antibiotics?

I understand — you don’t want to let them down. But you need a urine test, bloods and possibly a scan, and the paracetamol may need a treatment that protects your liver. Antibiotics alone over video would be unsafe. I can give you a fit note, and you could message your manager now.
model.why: Acknowledges the concern, explains why, helps with work

model.text: Please don’t take any more paracetamol or co-codamol, and don’t drive — could Priya take you, or a taxi? Take the tablet packets. If you get confused, very breathless, faint, or stop passing urine before you get there, call 999. I’ll ring you tomorrow. What will you do now?
model.why: Stop paracetamol, transport, 999 triggers, follow-up, teach-back

model.text: No more paracetamol, ask Priya to take me to A&E with the packets, 999 if I get worse. And message my boss.

social.t: Young professionals away for work often minimise illness. Helping her inform her manager removes a barrier to going.
A colleague nearby is a resource for transport and for checking on her.

legal.t: Prescribing codeine or antibiotics remotely without adequate assessment is unsafe here; document why face-to-face assessment was needed.

professional.t: A previous diagnosis (“my back”) anchors both patient and doctor. Re-take the history each time.

community.t: Nearest ED; NHS 24 (111) in Scotland; community pharmacist advice on combination analgesics in future.

redFlags: Tachycardia, low BP, confusion, reduced urine (sepsis)
psychosocial: Where she is and who is with her
core: Site and character of pain vs previous episode

playbook.diagnosis: Probable acute right pyelonephritis with features of possible sepsis (obstructed infected kidney to exclude); unintentional staggered paracetamol overdose (about 8 g/day for 2 days).
playbook.diagnosisLay: “This looks like a kidney infection that may be spreading, not your back — and you’ve accidentally taken too much paracetamol. Both need checking today.”

management.reflectIce: “You were expecting painkillers and physio, and you don’t want to let your team down. I’d be letting you down if I didn’t get you checked today.”
management.psychosocial: Message manager; fit note; colleague to accompany.
sharedPlan: Nearest ED today — urine, bloods, imaging as needed, antibiotics
Stop all paracetamol-containing products; take the packets; paracetamol level and LFTs
Do not drive — colleague or taxi
No codeine or physiotherapy referral now
safetyNet: 999 if confused, very breathless, faint, or not passing urine
Own GP review on return home

pitfalls.intro: The opening request is designed to anchor the candidate on mechanical back pain. Two hazards hide behind it.

items.fail: Asks back-pain red flags only and prescribes codeine.
items.why: Misses fever, rigors and loin pain — and the paracetamol excess.
items.fix: Ask where exactly, whether it differs from before, and about fever, urine and medicines.

items.fail: Prescribes cefalexin to a local pharmacy and safety-nets.
items.why: Possible sepsis and possible obstruction need face-to-face assessment and tests; the overdose needs bloods.
She may not go if the barrier is not addressed.
items.fix: Acknowledge it and help practically (fit note, message the manager).

wordPics.clearFail: Accepts “back flare”, prescribes codeine and refers to physio; no fever, urine or medicine history.
wordPics.fail: Suspects a kidney infection but prescribes antibiotics remotely, or sends her to ED without finding the paracetamol excess.
wordPics.pass: Recognises loin pain with systemic features, asks about urine, pregnancy and analgesics, finds the paracetamol excess, and sends her to the nearest ED today with clear advice not to drive and 999 triggers.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, plus: explains both problems simply, handles the work pressure and the antibiotic request skilfully, uses her colleague and the packets, and confirms the plan by teach-back with a follow-up call.

avoid.dont: “I’ll send codeine up and you can see how it goes.”
avoid.instead: “This pain is different from last time — let me ask a few more questions.”
“Co-codamol has paracetamol in it too, so you’ve had more than the safe amount — that needs a blood test.”
avoid.why: Accurate without blame; it was unintentional.

avoid.instead: “Please don’t drive — could Priya take you, or a taxi?”
avoid.why: Fever and rigors impair safe driving.
